title: Around the World in 80 Days

subtitle.text: Mr. Phileas Fogg was a mystery. No one knew how he had made his fortune, but there was no doubt that he was rich.
He was in his forties, tall, well-built, with handsome features.
He had light hair, pale skin, and excellent teeth.
He was one of the most prominent members of London's Reform Club, and yet he attracted little attention.
It was clear to those who knew him that Phileas Fogg was a traveler.
He was familiar with the world and knew the details of even the most remote areas of the earth.
It was also certain, however, that Mr. Fogg had not left London in many years.
He lived a quiet single life with no wife or children to keep him company, and his daily routine never changed.
On October 2, 1872, Mr. Fogg sat squarely in his armchair in his mansion on Savile Row.
His hands were resting on his knees, and his body was straight.
He was watching a complicated clock that told the seconds, minutes, hours, days, months, and years all at once.
A knock sounded at the front door, and before long, Mr. Fogg's servant, who was leaving that day, appeared.
"The new servant is here to see you, sir," he said.
Then a young man about thirty years old entered the room and bowed.
"You are a Frenchman, I believe," asked Phileas Fogg, "and your name is John?"
"Jean, if monsieur pleases," replied the newcomer.
"My name is Jean Passepartout. My surname suits me because I have a natural ability to move from one business to another.
I believe I'm honest, monsieur, and I've had several jobs.
I've been a singer, a circus acrobat, a tight-rope walker, a gymnastics teacher, and finally, a fireman in Paris."
"Well, Mr. Passepartout," said Mr. Fogg, "you have been well recommended to me.
I have heard good reports about you."
"Thank you, monsieur," said Passepartout. "I wish now to enjoy a quiet domestic life as a valet here in England.
I have heard that you are a most exact and settled gentleman, so I have come in the hope of living a tranquil life.
Maybe I will even forget the name of Passepartout."
"You know my conditions?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"Yes, monsieur," said Passepartout.
"Good! What time is it?" asked Mr. Fogg.
Taking a huge silver watch from his pocket, Passepartout replied, "Twenty-five minutes after eleven."
"Your watch is slow," said Mr. Fogg.
"Pardon me, monsieur, it is impossible," said Passepartout.
"It is four minutes too slow," said Mr. Fogg.
"No matter. It's enough only to mention the error.
Now from this moment, 29 minutes after 11 a.m., this Wednesday, the second of October, you are in my service."
Mr. Fogg stood up, and without a further word, he put on his hat and left.
Every day, at exactly 11:30 a.m., Mr. Fogg left his house and walked to the Reform Club.
He was so precise that he never appeared to be rushed or agitated in any way.
He was the most deliberate person in the world and always reached his destination at the very moment that he was due.
At half-past eleven, then, Passepartout found himself alone in the house on Savile Row.
He began an inspection and was pleased to find the house clean and arranged neatly.
When Passepartout reached the second floor, he recognized at once the room that was meant for him.
Hanging over the clock above the fireplace was the daily routine of the house, written on a card.
It explained Passepartout's duties, from eight in the morning, when Mr. Fogg got up, until half-past eleven, when Mr. Fogg left for his club.
It explained the tea and toast at 8:23, the shaving water at 9:37, and the washcloth, soap, and washbowl at 9:40.
In Mr. Fogg's closet each pair of pants, coat, and vest had a number on it.
This indicated the time of year and the season when it would be worn.
Mr. Fogg used the same system for his shoes as well.
Having inspected the house from top to bottom, Passepartout rubbed his hands together.
"This is just what I wanted!" he said.
"We will get along well together, Mr. Fogg and I!"
Meanwhile Mr. Phileas Fogg had put his right foot before his left foot 575 times
and his left foot before his right foot 576 times and reached the Reform Club.
He immediately went into the dining room and took his place at his usual table, which had already been set for him.
Phileas Fogg's lunch consisted of a broiled fish with sauce and a slice of roast beef garnished with mushrooms.
He also ate a rhubarb and gooseberry tart and a morsel of Cheshire cheese.
The entire meal was washed down with several cups of tea.
Mr. Fogg rose at thirteen minutes to one and went into the large hall.
He found his regular chair in his regular corner and happily sat down to pass the afternoon as he did every day:
quietly reading the newspapers amidst the comfortable and lavish surroundings of his club.
Hello. I am Jean Passepartout, and the year is 1872, during the Victorian Era.
London is the largest and most modern city on earth.
Its streets are very crowded with people and horse-drawn carriages.
Below the streets, trains, which were invented less than fifty years ago, travel through the London Underground.
A lot of great scientific discovery has occurred lately.
At night London's streets are now lit by gas lamps.
If you have an urgent message to send, you can send it by electronic wire, using Morse code.
Perhaps you've heard of Morse code? It uses a series of dots and dashes to relay information.
London is the capital not only of England but also of the vast British Empire.
Queen Victoria rules over almost one-quarter of the earth's land.
People often say, "The sun never sets on the British Empire."
That's because it's always daytime in at least one of the Queen's territories.
At Phileas Fogg's mansion Passepartout had read and memorized the card listing his master's daily routine.
He knew that Mr. Fogg would not be back until exactly midnight.
So Passepartout set about keeping himself busy until his services were needed again.
Passepartout had a pleasant face and a well-built, muscular body.
He had tumbled brown hair, blue eyes, and a ruddy complexion.
In his early years, Passepartout had been a sort of vagrant and was not at all brash or snobby.
He had already worked in ten English houses, but so far he had failed to find the peace he was looking for.
He was happy to have finally found a master who suited him.
Back at the Reform Club, shortly after six o'clock that evening, Mr. Fogg finished his dinner.
Then he joined five other club members for a game of whist.
Mr. Fogg was a regular player, and his evening card game was an unchanging part of his routine.
The men settled down at a table in front of a fire, and the conversation soon turned to current affairs.
"What about that robbery then?" asked one player.
"Oh, the bank will lose the money," replied another.
"The [i@Daily Telegraph@i] says that the thief is a gentleman," said Mr. Fogg as he set down his newspaper to pick up his cards.
"A man that makes off with fifty-five-thousand pounds is no gentleman!" said another.
"Possibly not," replied Mr. Fogg, "but he was reported to be a well-dressed gentleman with polished manners and a well-to-do air about him."
The conversation subsided as the men began their game.
When they paused to deal the cards for a second game, the conversation returned to the robbery.
"Where could the 'gentleman,' if that's what we must call him, go?" exclaimed one player.
"It would be very difficult to flee with all that money," said another.
"No country will be safe for him."
"Oh, I'm not sure about that," said another man. "The world is big enough."
"It was once," said Mr. Fogg, "but no longer.
It is now possible to go around the world in eighty days."
"That is true," said one man.
"Impossible," said another. "What if the trains stop running in India, or a storm delays a steamer? What then?"
"All accounted for and anticipated in eighty days," stated Mr. Fogg with confidence.
"I'd like to see you do it!" said the player sitting opposite him.
"I'd like nothing better than to do it," said Mr. Fogg, looking at him calmly.
"When?" asked the man.
"At once," said Mr. Fogg, smiling.
"It's absurd," cried another player. "Let's get on with the game!"
Suddenly the man who was about to deal put the cards down and spoke up.
"Fair enough, Mr. Fogg. I will wager four-thousand pounds on it!"
"I will too," said another, looking to the other players.
"And so will I," said another, and then another, until all five men agreed.
Mr. Fogg looked up from his cards and said, "I have a deposit of twenty- thousand pounds at the bank that I will gladly risk on it."
"Twenty-thousand pounds! Twenty-thousand pounds that you could lose by a single accidental delay?" asked the man who had bet first.
"The unforeseen does not exist," replied Mr. Fogg.
"But, Mr. Fogg," said the man. "Eighty days are only an estimate of the minimum time the journey can take."
"For this journey, that minimum will suffice," said Mr. Fogg.
"And in order not to exceed the eighty days," the man continued,
"you'll need to be very precise when transferring from trains to steamers and from steamers to trains."
"I will be [i@very@i] precise, gentlemen," said Mr. Fogg.
Phileas Fogg's card partners were both thrilled and concerned.
They were thrilled by a bet they felt certain to win.
But they were concerned that Mr. Fogg was risking a lot of money on a whim.
"If you are joking, we accept the joke and let you off," offered one man.
"A true Englishman doesn't joke when he is talking about something as serious as a wager," replied Mr. Fogg.
"I will bet twenty-thousand pounds against anyone that I can tour the world in eighty days or less. Do you accept?"
Hello, again! Gentlemen's clubs are private clubs for men from the English upper class.
In other words they are not for men like me! Ha-ha!
Members use gentleman's clubs almost as second homes.
They go to these clubs to relax, meet their friends, and enjoy delicious meals.
Mr. Fogg is a member of the Reform Club, and he spends most of his days there.
The Reform Club was founded in 1836.
Membership quickly grew to one thousand
and the club's governing committee commissioned an architect to design its current building, located at 104 Pall Mall.
This street actually has quite a few gentlemen's clubs along it.
The Reform Club is a splendid place.
Based on the Farnese Palace in Rome, its central hall is encircled by grand pillars and a spacious upper gallery.
It has a wonderful kitchen, which was designed according to the chef's specifications.
The Reform Club's library contains over fifty-thousand books!
The Reform Club was founded by a political party known as the Radicals, who embraced liberal political ideas.
So besides being a social club, it is also a political meeting place.
Members use the space to share news, hold meetings, plan campaign strategies, and conduct other party business.
Phileas Fogg's five whist opponents all looked at each other, nodded, and said unanimously, "We accept!"
Mr. Fogg's wager to travel around the world in eighty days was on!
"Good," said Phileas Fogg. "The train leaves for Dover at a quarter before nine. I will take it."
"This very evening?" one of the men said.
"Yes, this very evening!" said Mr. Fogg. He then took out his pocket almanac and added, "Today is Wednesday, October 2.
I shall be due in London, in this very room of the Reform Club, on Saturday December 21, at a quarter before 9:00 p.m.
If I am late, twenty-thousand pounds, now deposited in my name at Baring's Bank, will belong to you."
Then Mr. Fogg pulled out his checkbook and signed a check with his fountain pen.
"In fact, gentlemen," he said, "here is a check for the amount."
The men drafted a contract outlining the wager and everyone signed it.
During this whole exchange, Phileas Fogg maintained his usual cool composure.
He had not bet to win, but merely to live up to his word.
He had staked twenty-thousand pounds, half his fortune.
He thought he might have to spend the other half to carry out this difficult project.
The clock struck seven, and the group agreed to suspend the game so Mr. Fogg could prepare for his departure.
"It is unnecessary, gentlemen. I am quite ready now," was Mr. Fogg's response.
"It is your turn, I believe," he said to the man on his left.
So, after winning twenty guineas at whist and taking leave of his friends,
Phileas Fogg, at twenty-five minutes past seven, left the Reform Club and made his way home.
When Mr. Fogg arrived home, Passepartout was surprised.
His master was not due until exactly midnight.
Mr. Fogg immediately went to his room and called for his servant.
But Passepartout did not reply. Mr. Fogg could not be calling for him. It was not the right hour!
"Passepartout," repeated Mr. Fogg, without raising his voice.
Passepartout arrived.
"I've called you twice," said his master.
"But it is not midnight," said Passepartout, showing Mr. Fogg his watch.
"I know that. I don't blame you, but we start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes," said Mr. Fogg.
"You are going to leave home?" asked Passepartout with a puzzled look on his face.
"Yes," said his master. "We are going around the world."
Passepartout opened his eyes wide, and looked like he might collapse. "Around the world?" he murmured.
"In eighty days," replied Mr. Fogg. "So we haven't a moment to lose."
"But I must pack our trunks!" Passepartout said.
"We will have no trunks, only a carpetbag with two shirts and three pairs of socks for me, and the same for you.
We will buy our clothes on the way," said Mr. Fogg.
Passepartout tried to reply but couldn't. He left Mr. Fogg's room, climbed the stairs to his own room, and fell into the closest chair.
Was his master a fool? No. Was this a joke? It didn't seem so.
They were going to Dover and then to Calais, in France.
Passepartout thought a moment later. After all, Passepartout had been away from France for five years.
He would not be sorry to see his native soil again.
Remembering there was no time to waste, Passepartout packed the carpetbag and was ready by eight o'clock.
Mr. Fogg was ready as well. He was carrying the railway and steamer timetable under his arm.
He then took the carpetbag, opened it, and slipped a huge roll of bank notes inside it.
"You have forgotten nothing?" he asked Passepartout.
"No, nothing, sir," replied Passepartout.
"Good! Take this carpetbag," Mr. Fogg said, handing it to Passepartout.
"Take good care of it because there is twenty-thousand pounds in it."
Passepartout nearly dropped the bag, as if the twenty- thousand pounds were as heavy as gold.
Mr. Fogg and Passepartout then left the house, locked the door securely, and took a cab to Charing Cross railway station.
The cab stopped in front of the station at 8:25, exactly twenty- five-minutes before the train was to depart.
Oh my! I had thought I would be settling down for a nice, quiet life.
But suddenly I found out I was about to travel around the world—and in eighty days!
Mr. Fogg told me that our trip will start in Dover.
Located at the southeastern tip of England, Dover is famous for its tall, white cliffs, which are made of pure white chalk.
In fact, these white cliffs gave England its most ancient name: Albion, which means "white."
Dover is one of the busiest places to cross the English Channel.
Traffic through this port town has boomed since the railway connected it to London.
People traveling on the London-Dover train can take the 21-mile ferry ride across the English Channel to Calais, France.
There they can hop on the Calais-Paris train.
So far our journey around the world sounds easy, right? Well, we'll see what happens next!
Mr. Fogg paid the cabman and was about to enter the train station when a poor beggar approached him.
She was carrying a child in her arms, her bare feet were smeared with mud, and her clothes were old and torn.
She asked Mr. Fogg for some money for food.
Mr. Fogg took out the twenty guineas he had won that very evening at whist and handed them to her, saying, "Here, my good woman.
I'm glad that I met you." Then he continued on his way.
Passepartout was touched by his master's generosity, and he entered the station with a tear in his eye.
Mr. Fogg quickly bought two first-class tickets for Paris.
As he and Passepatout were crossing the platform, Mr. Fogg saw his five friends from the Reform Club.
"Well, gentlemen," he said. "I'm off, and you can examine my passport when I get back.
You will be able to judge then whether I completed the journey."
"Oh, that is quite unnecessary, Mr. Fogg," said one man politely.
"We trust your word as a gentleman of honor."
"You do remember when you are due back in London?" asked another man.
"In eighty days, on Saturday, December 21, 1872, at 8:45 p.m.," said Mr. Fogg. "Good-bye, gentlemen."
And with that, Phileas Fogg and Passepartout boarded the train and seated themselves in the first-class carriage.
Five-minutes later the train whistled, and then glided out of the station.
Phileas Fogg suspected that his departure from London would create a lively sensation. He was right.
The news of the extraordinary bet spread through the Reform Club and sparked excited conversation among its members.
The news quickly got into the newspapers around London, and the "tour of the world" was soon being talked about all over town.
Some people supported Mr. Fogg and believed his journey would be a success.
But many thought he was insane for betting so much money on a journey he could not possibly complete in eighty days.
Many of the newspapers claimed Mr. Fogg's project was madness.
Only the [i@Daily Telegraph@i] supported his adventure.
Soon the members of the Reform Club weren't the only ones to place wagers on Phileas Fogg's journey.
His name began appearing in the betting books as if he were a racehorse!
Five days after his departure, an article appeared in the bulletin of the Royal Geographical Society.
Everything, it said, was against the travelers.
There would be obstacles imposed by humans and by nature.
Furthermore, Fogg's success would depend on a miraculous agreement of trains and steamers' departure and arrival times.
Mr. Fogg might be able to depend on trains arriving on time in Europe, where distances were relatively short.
But when he was trying to cross India in three days, and the United States in seven, transportation would not be as reliable.
Surely there would be problems with machinery, trains running off the tracks, collisions, and bad weather.
Still, as Phileas Fogg rode the train out of London, he was relaxed and confident in his first-class carriage,
unconcerned about any of the problems that could interrupt his journey.
Passepartout, however, had still not recovered from the shock of being whisked away on such short notice.
He clung mechanically to the carpetbag filled with money and stared straight ahead without seeing a thing.
As the train was speeding through Sydenham, just outside London, Passepartout suddenly uttered a cry of despair.
"What's the matter?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"Alas!" cried Passepartout. "In my hurry I forgot . . ."
"What?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"To turn off the gas in my room!" said Passepartout.
"Very well, young man," returned Mr. Fogg coolly. "It will burn . . . at your expense."
Passepartout looked down in embarrassment. It was his fault, after all.
After arriving in Calais, they traveled by train to Paris and then through the Alps to Turin in northern Italy.
They traversed Italy to Brindisi, at the heel of Italy's boot, where they boarded the ship [i@Mongolia@i] and sailed for Suez.
So Mr. Fogg and I had just caught the train from Paris, France, to Brindisi, a port in the south of Italy.
What a long trip it was! Although I must say, it was extremely comfortable.
After all, this is known as the "golden age" of rail travel.
Train travel is now more popular and comfortable than ever before.
Train tracks first appeared in Europe in the 1500s, but the "train" was a wagon pulled along the track by horses.
In 1804 an English steam engine pulled train cars with passengers for the first time.
Early steam engines like this were often called "iron horses."
I'm just glad I didn't have to "feed" it the coal it needed! What a tough and dirty job!
The first passenger trains were pretty rough.
They seldom traveled more than 18 miles per hour, passengers sat on wooden benches, and meals were eaten quickly in dining halls at train stations.
Thankfully, train travel has improved a lot since then.
By the 1860s trains could travel at around 99 miles per hour, and no more wooden benches!
Passengers now have a choice of first, second, or third class.
First class is like a hotel on wheels!
The rooms are large and luxurious, and the dining car resembles a fancy restaurant.
There are also bars and lounges where passengers can relax, and watch the countryside go by.
Phileas Fogg and his eighty-day adventure were soon overshadowed by other events.
A report appeared describing the "gentleman" robber who had stolen the fifty-five-thousand pounds,
and the newspapers were caught up once again with the details of the robbery.
The police were looking for suspects all over Europe.
One agent in the vast manhunt was a short, slightly built man with a nervous, intelligent face and bright eyes.
Detective Fix had been sent to Suez to watch every person who arrived there.
His instructions were to investigate any suspicious characters and certainly anyone who resembled the thief.
Fix stood on the dock, looking out at the water.
His eyebrows twitched nonstop, which was always a sign of his impatience.
"Excuse me," Fix called to a passing sailor.
"Can you tell me if the [i@Mongolia@i] is expected on time?"
"It's a very punctual ship, it is," replied the sailor.
"It has won awards for its speed."
Fix felt that he had a good sense for spotting criminals.
He had arrested plenty in his time.
If the thief were on board the [i@Mongolia@i], he wouldn't sneak past Fix.
"What a magnificent robbery it was," Fix thought.
"Fifty-five-thousand pounds! And by a man who resembles an honest gentleman.
It's extraordinary! Thieves are getting to be bold nowadays.
But then those fellows never have rascally faces, or they would be arrested immediately.
No, I'm sure this thief looks honest, and I'm going to find him."
The [i@Mongolia@i] was stopping in Suez for only a few hours to refuel, so Fix did not have a lot of time to spot his man.
Fix took his position, and when the ship arrived and the passengers disembarked, he carefully examined every face that passed.
One of the passengers vigorously pushed his way through the crowd and came right up to Fix.
The stranger held out a passport, explaining that he wished to have it stamped, and asked directions to the British consulate.
Fix instinctively took the passport and read the description of its owner.
His eyebrows lifted in surprise. The description perfectly matched the bank thief.
"Is this your passport?" asked Fix.
The stranger was Passepartout, and the passport in his hand belonged to Phileas Fogg.
"No, it's my master's," replied Passepartout.
"And where is your master now?" asked Fix.
"He stayed onboard," said Passepartout.
"He must go to the consul's office in person," said Fix.
"And where is the consulate? My master won't be pleased to be disturbed," replied Passepartout, frowning.
"The consulate is not far. Have you or your master been to Suez before?" asked Fix, hoping for more information about the owner of the passport.
"I have not," said Passepartout. "And I do not expect to see much of it.
In fact, I expected my master to stop in Paris to see the sights.
But all I saw of that city was seen as we rushed from one train station to another."
"You are in a great hurry then?" asked Fix, growing more curious.
"I am not, but my master is," said Passepartout.
"By the way, I must buy some shirts and shoes.
We were in such a rush, we left with only a carpetbag."
"But where is your master going?" asked Fix.
"He is going around the world in eighty days," said Passepartout.
"He says it's a wager, but between you and me, I don't believe a word of it!
I think he has another reason for the trip."
"Ah! Mr. Fogg is a character, is he? Is he rich?" asked Fix as his eyes lit up.
"No doubt," replied Passepartout. "He is carrying an enormous sum in brand-new banknotes with him."
"And have you known your master long?" asked Fix, his voice filled with excitement.
"Why, no, I entered his service the same day we left London.
I will fetch him now and bring him to the consulate," Passepartout said.
Passepartout's words had deeply intrigued the detective.
Mr. Fogg had departed hastily from London, quite soon after the robbery.
And the large sum of bank notes he carried was unusual, as was his peculiar eagerness to reach distant countries.
All of it fit Fix's theory of the robber.
Fix rapidly made his way to the British consulate.
He was sure there would be a large reward for capturing such a bold criminal.
The detective burst into the consul's office and exclaimed, "Consul, there's a thief on board the [i@Mongolia.@i]
He will be here any moment. You must detain him!"
The race against time was on! We still had a long way to go, but luckily the Suez Canal had opened in 1869.
The Suez Canal was the fastest way to go from Europe to India and Asia.
Before it was built, goods had to be unloaded from ships and carried overland.
Otherwise ships had to sail around all of Africa, and that was a rough and dangerous journey.
I'm glad we didn't go that way!
The Suez Canal is located in Egypt and links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.
People think the ancient Egyptians first built a canal there nearly four-thousand years ago.
Since then the canal has been destroyed, rebuilt, and destroyed again.
Finally proper construction began in 1859, and the canal was completed in 1869.
It is 101 miles long and about 984 feet wide at its narrowest point.
Over 1.5 million people were forced to work on the canal, mostly by hand.
Would you like to dig a canal by hand? I certainly wouldn't!
The consul looked at Fix in surprise and said, "There's a thief on board the [i@Mongolia@i]? Are you certain?"
"Consul, I have no doubt. I have spotted my man," said Fix with conviction.
"He passes himself off as an eccentric, rich man who is going around the world in eighty days.
When he arrives to have his passport stamped, you must hold him here!"
"He is coming to have a visa entered in his passport?" asked the consul.
"Yes, but I hope you will not issue the visa," said Fix.
"Why not? If the passport is genuine, I have no right to refuse."
"Criminals such as this man use passports to flee the law.
You must keep him here!" replied Fix, his frustration growing.
"I cannot hold a man, no matter how sure you are of his guilt, without a warrant.
Surely you are aware of that," replied the consul, shaking his head.
"Perhaps this Mr. Fogg won't even come here if he is indeed the person you suppose him to be.
A robber doesn't like to leave traces of his flight behind him, you know.
Besides, he is not obligated to have his passport stamped anyway."
"If he is as shrewd as I think he is, consul, he will—" began Fix.
But before he could finish, someone knocked on the door.
Fix quickly hid himself in a corner of the room as Passepartout and his master entered the office.
From his hiding place, Fix observed as the consul took Mr. Fogg's documents and read them carefully.
"You are Mr. Phileas Fogg?" asked the consul.
"I am," said Fogg.
"And this is your servant?" asked the consul.
"He is," said Fogg. "A Frenchman named Passepartout."
"You are from London?" asked the consul.
"Yes," said Fogg.
"And you are going . . . ?" asked the consul.
"To Bombay," replied Mr. Fogg.
"Very good, sir," said the consul. "You know that no passport is required and a visa would be meaningless?"
"I know it, sir," replied Phileas Fogg.
"But I wish to prove, by your visa, that I traveled via Suez."
"Very well, sir." The consul proceeded to sign and date the passport, and then added his official seal.
Mr. Fogg paid the fee, bowed, and went out, followed by Passepartout.
After leaving the consul's office, Mr. Fogg returned to the dock and gave some instructions to Passepartout.
Then he made his way to his cabin on the [i@Mongolia@i] and picked up his travel journal.
In this journal a detailed itinerary listed all the major stopping points on Mr. Fogg's route:
Paris, Brindisi, Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Singapore, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, and finally London.
Next to each was written the expected day and time of arrival with a space for noting the actual arrival time and the hours gained or lost.
As a result Mr. Fogg always knew whether he was behind or in advance of his schedule.
He added his newest entry: [i@Reached Suez Wednesday, October 9, at 11:00 a.m.@i]
[i@Total of hours spent: 158; or in days: six and a half.@i]
As Fogg closed his journal and put away his pen, he observed that he had neither gained nor lost time.
He sat down quietly to eat breakfast in his cabin, never once thinking of visiting the town.
After seeing Mr. Fogg in person, Fix was convinced that Fogg was the culprit.
Fogg fit the description of the robber perfectly.
"Everything adds up," Fix said to himself.
"His leaving London so quickly, his hiring a new servant the very same day . . . It's all very suspicious."
Fix quickly decided that he must follow Mr. Fogg.
It was his duty, after all, and the reward for catching such a cunning criminal as this supposed gentleman would be his. Fix turned to the consul.
"I must leave at once. I am going to telegraph the police in London.
I must follow this man!" he said.
The detective thanked the consul for his help and left.
Fix went immediately to the telegraph office and sent the following wire: [i@Suez to London.@i]
[i@Rowan, Commissioner of Police, Scotland Yard. I've found the bank robber, Phileas Fogg.@i]
[i@Send an arrest warrant to Bombay without delay. Fix, Detective.@i]
A quarter of an hour later, with a small bag in his hand, Fix boarded the [i@Mongolia.@i]
During our journey it's my job to keep track of Mr. Fogg's passport.
If I lose it, I will be in big trouble!
Whenever you travel abroad, you must bring a passport with you.
A passport is a document issued by your country for the purpose of overseas travel.
The word "passport" most likely comes from the medieval word for the gate, or [i@porte@i], of a city.
Notice my name, Passepartout, looks a lot like the word "passport."

The telegram that Detective Fix sent to Scotland Yard had an instant effect on opinion in London.
Suddenly Phileas Fogg was no longer an eccentric rich man who had accepted a wager to travel around the world.
Now he was a suspected gentleman bank robber!
Betting on his grand adventure ceased, and his name was dropped from the betting books.
Instead his name filled the papers as speculation grew about his connection to the theft of the fifty-five-thousand pounds.
Mr. Fogg, oblivious to the telegram or any news at home, was focused just on his goal.
In fact, after breakfast, and while Passepartout was shopping for necessities in Suez, Mr. Fogg went to see the captain of the [i@Mongolia@i].
"My good sir," began Mr. Fogg, "may I have a word with you regarding our voyage to Bombay?"
"I can speak with you only briefly, sir, as we are set to sail in less than an hour," said the captain.
"What I have to say is brief," replied Mr. Fogg.
"I am in a great hurry and would be obliged if you could reach Bombay in the shortest time possible.
In fact, I am willing to offer you a considerable sum if you arrive in Bombay more than a day ahead of schedule."
The captain was surprised by Mr. Fogg's request but had no trouble agreeing to make haste.
When Passepartout returned to the [i@Mongolia@i] shortly before it set sail, Mr. Fogg was waiting for him.
Detective Fix was also on board, planning Mr. Fogg's arrest.
The detective hoped that the warrant for Mr. Fogg would be ready when the boat arrived in Bombay.
After passing through the famous canal at Suez, the [i@Mongolia@i] entered the Red Sea.
Winds from the African coast made the waves boisterous, and many passengers speedily disappeared below deck.
As he watched the wind and the billowing waves, was Phileas Fogg anxious about the steamer's progress?
As calmly as if he were sitting in his Reform Club, he passed through the Red Sea with indifference.
When the weather calmed, he did not view the historic villages on the coast.
The [i@Mongolia@i] ploughed on into the Arabian Sea, and he paid no attention.
He ate four hearty meals a day, slept soundly every night, and passed his time playing whist with other enthusiastic card players like himself.
Passepartout, however, thoroughly enjoyed watching the scenery.
He spent hours every day lounging on the deck and taking in his surroundings.
He ate his meals in the forward cabin.
It was there one day where he spotted the obliging person with whom he had talked in Suez.
"If I am not mistaken," Passepartout said, approaching Detective Fix, "you are the gentleman who kindly helped me in Suez."
"Ah! I recognize you. Yes, you are the servant of the unusual Englishman," said Fix with a smile.
"Exactly, monsieur," said Passepartout.
"Fix, my name is Fix."
"Monsieur Fix, I am charmed to meet you. Where are you bound?" asked Passepartout.
"Like you, to Bombay," replied Fix.
"Splendid. I have just finished my lunch," said Passepartout, as he reached into his pocket and pulled out his large silver watch.
"It is now one o'clock. Would you like to walk around the deck with me?"
"Yes, I would. But your watch does not tell the right time, sir. It is slow," said Fix.
"My watch? It is a family watch," said Passepartout.
"It has come down to me from my great-grandfather! It doesn't vary five minutes in a year. It's a perfect timepiece."
"I see," said Fix. "I believe you have kept London time, which is two hours behind that of the Suez.

"Regulate my watch?" asked Passepartout. "Never!"
"Well, then, it will not agree with the sun," said Fix.
"That is a problem for the sun, monsieur!"
And with a defiant gesture, Passepartout returned his watch to his pocket.
Fix decided to change the subject and in the most casual tone asked, "Is Mr. Fogg getting on well?"
"Quite well," said Passepartout. "And I am too.
It must be the sea air. I am eating like a famished giant."
Fix smiled, and their amiable conversation continued with innocent topics.
During the crossing Fix and Passepartout got into the habit of meeting and chatting regularly.
Fix often offered Passepartout a whiskey or beer in the steamer's bar, and Passepartout never failed to accept his generosity.
The [i@Mongolia@i] was due in Bombay on October 22. But it arrived on October 20.
So Mr. Fogg had gained two days, which he calmly entered in his travel journal after paying the captain his reward.
Fix, however, was not as happy.
As soon as the ship docked, Fix hastily made his way to the local police station in search of the warrant for Fogg.
But being two days ahead of schedule, he knew the chances of finding it waiting for him were slim.

Detective Fix introduced himself at the Bombay police headquarters.
He had hurried there first thing in the morning, as soon as the [i@Mongolia@i] had docked.
He inquired if the warrant for Fogg's arrest had arrived from London yet, but it had not.
"If the [i@Mongolia@i] were not two days ahead of schedule, I wouldn't be in this situation," Fix explained to the Bombay director of police.
He urged the director to issue an order for the arrest of Mr. Fogg, but the director refused.
"The matter concerns the London office," the director explained, "and only London can deliver the order."
Fix fumed, but he did not insist.
"Bombay is far enough from London so that a fleeing bank robber will not worry about being seen," he thought.
So Mr. Fogg would probably stay in Bombay for a while, and the warrant would arrive before his departure.
In the meantime Fix was determined not to lose sight of his mysterious suspect.
He hurried through the crowded streets back to the boat.
He wanted to be there when Mr. Fogg disembarked.
Mr. Fogg, for his part, left the steamer in the afternoon.
After saying good-bye to his whist partners, he descended the gangway, carrying the carpetbag in his hand.
On the shore he instructed Passepartout to attend to several errands, but urged him to be at the train station at eight o'clock and not a minute late.
Then, with steps as regular as the ticking of a watch, Mr. Fogg walked to the passport office.
After receiving a visa, he turned his steps to the train station, where he planned to have dinner and wait for the eight o'clock train to Calcutta.
Passepartout, like the detective, had thought his master would stay in Bombay at least for a few days.
When he heard his master's orders to meet at the train station, he realized that they were going to continue without delay.
He purchased the shirts and shoes his master had requested and took a leisurely stroll through the strange sights of Bombay.
Many nationalities crowded the streets:
Persians with pointed caps, long-robed Armenians, Indians wearing turbans, and many others in bright robes of red and orange.
In a market he saw a procession of dancers clothed in rose- colored gowns looped with gold and silver.
They danced airily through the streets to the sound of tambourines.
Passepartout had never seen anything like them before.
Passepartout followed the dancers through winding streets and lanes.
After a while he realized that his curiosity had led him farther from the center of the city than he had intended.
When he turned back to head to the train station, he noticed a magnificent Indian temple on nearby Malabar Hill.
It was too splendid to pass up, and he climbed the hill, seized with a desire to see its interior.
Passepartout, however, did not realize that it was forbidden for Christians to enter certain Indian temples,
and that even the faithful must leave their shoes outside.
The British government severely punished anyone who disregarded the practices of India's religions.
Meaning no harm, Passepartout went in like a simple tourist and was soon lost in admiration of the incredible ornamentation.
"I have never seen anything so magnificent!" he was thinking when suddenly he was knocked to the stone floor.
He looked up. Three angry priests jumped on him and tore off his shoes.
They began to beat him, exclaiming loudly.
"Help, help, they are stealing my shoes, someone help me!" screamed Passepartout.
He got to his feet again and wasted no time in knocking down two of the priests
before rushing out of the pagoda as fast as his legs would carry him.
When Passepartout finally arrived at the station, he was hatless and shoeless.
In the fight he had also lost the package with the newly purchased shirts and shoes.
It was five minutes before eight o'clock.
Fix had followed Mr. Fogg and was on the platform, having decided to follow him to Calcutta and farther, if necessary.
Listening from behind a newspaper, he heard Passepartout explain his adventure to his master.
Phileas Fogg was very annoyed by Passepartout's misadventure, but all he said was, "I hope that this will not happen again."
He turned his back and stepped onto the train.
Passepartout followed his master without a word.
Fix was about to enter a different train car when an idea struck him.
"I'll stay!" announced Fix to himself. "An offense has been committed on Indian soil. I've got my man!"
Just then the locomotive gave a sharp screech, and the train moved into the darkness of the Indian night.
Well, I learned my lesson about visiting temples in India.
Next time I travel, I'll be sure to learn more about local customs first!

There are many different forms of Hinduism, but most Hindus believe in a spiritual entity called Brahman.
Brahman is the supreme universal spirit in Hinduism.
Hindus worship in a [i@mandir@i] or temple.
Hinduism contains many distinct deities, so different [i@mandirs@i] are dedicated to different deities.
It's not just people who visit these temples.

When you go inside a [i@mandir@i], you must remember to be respectful.

The train from Bombay to Calcutta set out punctually at 8:00 p.m.
Among the passengers, to Mr. Fogg's delight, was Sir Francis Cromarty, a fellow whist player from the [i@Mongolia.@i]
Sir Francis had made India his home and was returning after a trip to England.
He asked to sit with Mr. Fogg, and they quickly fell into friendly conversation.
Sir Francis had never seen Mr. Fogg take in the sights during the boat voyage, and he noticed that on the train his companion was no different.
Phileas Fogg talked with Sir Francis, ignoring Passepartout.
He never looked out the window and didn't comment on the scenery at all.
"Does the man have any sense of the beauties of nature?" he wondered.
On the [i@Mongolia@i] Mr. Fogg had explained to Sir Francis the reason for his trip around the world.
Sir Francis thought the extravagant bet was a pointless eccentricity. "It lacks common sense!" he thought.
"The way this strange gentleman is going on, he will leave this world without having done anything good for himself or for anyone else."
He watched Mr. Fogg enter their departure from Bombay in his travel journal.
"Some years ago, Mr. Fogg," said Sir Francis, "you would have met a delay at this point, which probably would have lost you your wager."
"How so, Sir Francis?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"The railway stopped at the base of these mountains, which the passengers were obliged to cross in hand-carried carts, called palanquins.
Then they would board another train in Kandallah, on the other side."
"Such a delay would not have thrown off my plans in the least," replied Mr. Fogg.
"I have foreseen the likelihood of certain obstacles."
"But, Mr. Fogg," continued Sir Francis, "you do run the risk of having some difficulty about your servant's adventure at the pagoda."
Passepartout, his feet wrapped in a blanket, was sound asleep, with no idea that the men were talking about him.
"The government is very severe about that kind of offense.
It takes particular care that the religious customs of the Indians are respected. If your servant were caught . . ."
"Very well, Sir Francis," replied Mr. Fogg.
"If Passepartout had been caught, he would have been condemned and punished, and then he would have quietly returned to Europe.
It wouldn't have stopped me from completing my journey, nor would it have delayed me in the least!"
After this exchange the men fell silent.
During the night the train left the mountains behind.
Passepartout woke the next morning, and when he looked out his window, he saw the splendor of the great Indian subcontinent.
The train passed cotton, coffee, nutmeg, clove, and pepper plantations.
The fertile land was watered by many rivers and streams.
He saw picturesque low houses and marvelous temples surrounded by groves of palm trees.
Further on, the train entered a vast jungle that extended to the horizon.
The jungle was inhabited by snakes and tigers, which fled at the noise of the train.
Elephants with pensive eyes gazed at the train as it passed.
At half past 12, the train stopped at Burhampoor, where Passepartout was able to purchase some Indian slippers ornamented with false pearls.
Back on the train, the sights from the car window entranced Passepartout.
His old vagabond nature was coming back to him, and he recalled all the fantastic ideas of his youth.
He monitored the train's progress anxiously, getting impatient whenever it slowed or paused.
At eight o'clock the train stopped in the middle of a clearing where there were several huts and workmen's cabins.
The conductor passed through the cars and shouted, "Passengers will get out here!"
Phileas Fogg looked at Sir Francis for an explanation, but Sir Francis had no idea what was going on.
Passepartout, also surprised, rushed out of the car to see what the problem was.
He speedily returned, crying, "Monsieur, no more railway! No more railway!"
"What do you mean?" asked Sir Francis.
"I mean to say that the train isn't going on," said Passepartout, breathless.
Sir Francis immediately stepped out and, with Mr. Fogg following calmly behind, walked over to the conductor.
"Where are we?" asked Sir Francis.
"At the village of Kholby," replied the conductor.
"Do we stop here?" asked Sir Francis.
"Certainly," said the conductor. "The railway isn't finished."
"What! Not finished?" cried Sir Francis.
"There are still fifty miles of track to be laid from here to Allahabad," said the conductor.
"But you sell tickets from Bombay to Calcutta," said Sir Francis with exasperation.
"Yes," said the conductor. "But the passengers know they must find their own transport from Kholby to Allahabad."
Sir Francis was furious. Passepartout was angry enough to knock the conductor down.
They both turned to Mr. Fogg, who regarded them as calmly as ever.
As I sat on that train from Bombay to Calcutta, I never stopped looking out the window, except to sleep—ha-ha!
India is such a lush green country, and I saw so many plantations growing all sorts of crops.
By colonizing India and setting up railways, the British have been able to turn India into a center of commercial agriculture.
The three most important crops in India are coffee, indigo, and tea.
Tea is especially important. There are over three- hundred tea plantations in India!
They produce three-thousand tons of the stuff!
It's a shame though. Despite all that rich, fertile land and all those crops, many Indians are starving to death.
The crops are exported by Great Britain and sold overseas for profit.
"Sir Francis," said Mr. Fogg quietly, "we will look around for some transport to Allahabad."
"Mr. Fogg, this delay is to your disadvantage!" said Sir Francis.
"No, Sir Francis, it was foreseen," replied Fogg.
"What!" cried Sir Francis. "You knew that the railway—"
"Not at all," said Mr. Fogg. "But I knew that some obstacle would come up eventually.
Nothing is lost. I have two days, which I have gained, to sacrifice.
A steamer leaves Calcutta for Hong Kong at noon on the twenty-fifth.
This is the twenty-second so we shall reach Calcutta in time."
There was nothing Sir Francis could say to such a confident response.
The three men went separate ways to search the village for a vehicle.
Unfortunately, while they had been talking with the conductor,
the other passengers had already hired all the available wagons, carriages, and ponies.
Sir Francis and Mr. Fogg returned to the train with no luck.
Passepartout, however, returned from his search with a suggestion.
"Monsieur, I think I have found transport for us," he said.
"What would that be?" asked Fogg.
"An elephant!" said Passepartout. "It belongs to an Indian man who lives close by."
"Let's go and see the elephant," replied Mr. Fogg.
Passepartout led them to a small hut, near which a tall elephant stood behind a high gate.
The elephant's owner said its name was Kiouni, Mr. Fogg resolved immediately to hire him and offered ten pounds an hour.
The owner, however, refused and kept refusing every time Mr. Fogg raised his offer.
When Fogg offered forty pounds an hour, the owner still wouldn't agree.
Mr. Fogg, without getting the least bit upset, proposed to purchase the elephant completely.
He offered one thousand pounds but was refused again.
Passepartout listened in amazement as his master continued to raise the price.
Finally the man agreed to sell the elephant for two thousand pounds.
Mr. Fogg paid with bank notes from the carpetbag.
Kiouni was led out and equipped for the journey.
After hiring a guide and purchasing a few provisions, they set off at a quick pace.
Instead of following the wide, curving path that workers had cleared for the railway, their guide led them directly through the jungle.
Growls from panthers and the chatter of monkeys occasionally broke the jungle's stillness.
After a day of travelling, they stopped for the night.
The guide lit a fire, and they prepared a supper.
They ate hungrily and were snoring loudly soon after.
The journey started again at six o'clock the next morning.
Kiouni resumed his quick pace, and their guide said they might reach Allahabad that evening.
Fogg and his companions continued without any unpleasant encounters.
The journey seemed on the point of success when the elephant became restless and stopped. It was four o'clock.
"What's the matter?" asked Sir Francis.
"I'm not sure, sir," replied the guide, listening carefully.
A sound was coming through the thick bushes.
The guide jumped down, tied the elephant to a tree, and disappeared into the dense brush.
Mr. Fogg waited patiently without a word. The sound grew closer—it was a rhythmic concert of human voices and musical instruments.
The guide returned in a rush. "A procession of Brahmins is coming this way," he said. "We must hide!"
Through the branches of thick foliage, they watched the procession pass.
Behind a tall leader danced a group of bare-chested priests, their bodies striped with dark red mud or paint.
A young woman followed, led by four men in sumptuous Oriental clothes.
Each was armed with a curved sword at his waist.
The woman's neck, ears, arms, hands, and toes were loaded with jewels, bracelets, and rings.
She seemed weak, as if only half-awake, and two guards held her arms.
Musicians playing tambourines and cymbals followed at the end of the procession.
After the Brahmins had passed, Sir Francis said, "It is a [i@suttee,@i] a voluntary human sacrifice.
The woman we have just seen will be burned alive tomorrow at dawn.
Her husband has died, and she is to pass into the afterlife with him."
"That is true," said the guide. "But not all suttees are voluntary. Everyone in Kholby has heard about this suttee.
This young widow is not willing. She has been drugged so that she won't resist her fate."
The guide climbed onto the neck of Kiouni and prepared to continue their journey.
Mr. Fogg said, "Suppose we save the woman."
"Save the woman, Mr. Fogg?" said Sir Francis.
"I have 12 extra hours, which I can devote to saving this woman," said Fogg.
"You are a man of heart!" said Sir Francis.
"Sometimes," replied Mr. Fogg quietly. "When I have the time."
What a day that was! Riding an elephant through the jungle and finding a young woman about to be burned alive!
Although the majority of Indian widows are not burned, an Indian woman can never marry again if her husband dies.
According to Indian tradition, she has to shave her head and wear a white sari.
And it is quite common for young girls to be married to older men.
So if a young girl’s husband dies, she will wind up having to spend most of her life all alone.
Widows are also seen as a bad omen.
They are usually banished from their families, and many of them go to the city of Vrindavan, where they can work in the city's numerous temples.
Because of this, Vrindavan is sometimes called "the city of widows."
Attempting to rescue the young widow would be a bold undertaking, maybe even an impossible one.
But Mr. Fogg did not hesitate, and Sir Francis was an enthusiastic ally.
Passepartout was ready for anything, and even the guide was on their side.
"Where are they taking her?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"To the pagoda of Pillaji, two miles from here," said the guide.
"The woman will spend the night there, and the sacrifice will take place at the first light of dawn."
The guide looked at the group of rescuers.
"It is certain that we shall risk not only our lives but horrible tortures if we are caught!"
"That is foreseen," said Mr. Fogg. "I think we must wait until night before acting."
"I agree," said Sir Francis.
Their guide gave an account of the woman.
"She is the daughter of a wealthy Bombay merchant and received an excellent English education.
Her name is Aouda. While still very young, she was left an orphan and was married against her will to an old rajah.
When he died, she escaped, knowing the fate that awaited her.
But she was captured. That is why she is under such heavy guard now."
The guide's story strengthened the determination of Mr. Fogg and his friends.
As soon as night fell, the guide led them deeper into the thick jungle.
They came to an area lit by torches.
A group of Indians were sleeping outside a wide brick wall that enclosed the tall pagoda.
Guards with swords marched back and forth before the doors.
The rescuers hid themselves and waited, hoping the guards would fall asleep.
After midnight, when it was clear that the guards were going to patrol all night, Fogg and his companions sneaked around to the back of the pagoda.
With two sturdy knives that their guide had brought, Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis worked quietly at the loose bricks of the wall.
They managed to dislodge a few and then found they could remove the other bricks with their hands.
Their plan was to open a hole large enough for Aouda to slip through.
Suddenly a cry arose from inside the pagoda.
Mr. Fogg and his friends escaped into the jungle just as the guards ran to the back of the pagoda.
Sir Francis shook his fists, Passepartout was furious, and the guide grimaced with rage.
How could they save Aouda now? The tranquil Mr. Fogg waited, revealing no emotion.
"We can do nothing but go on our way," whispered Sir Francis.
"He is right. We must go," said the guide.
"Stop," said Fogg. "I am not due at Allahabad before noon tomorrow.
We may get another chance to rescue her."
"What is this cool Englishman thinking?" Sir Francis wondered.
"Is he planning to boldly snatch the woman from her executioners at the very moment of the sacrifice?"
It was hard to believe that the calm Phileas Fogg could attempt something so desperate.
They crept around the outskirts of the clearing and made their way back to the doors of the pagoda.
Concealed by the jungle, Fogg and his companions watched through the night.
Passepartout climbed into the branches of a tree.
While he was perched there, an idea struck him, and the more he considered it, the more firmly it lodged in his brain.
The lengthening shadows announced the approach of day, and the Indians sleeping outside the pagoda woke up.
Tambourines sounded and chanting began. The hour of the sacrifice had come.
The doors of the pagoda swung open.
Aouda was led out, struggling in the clutches of two large guards.
Sir Francis' heart throbbed, and he seized Mr. Fogg's hand.
He was surprised to discover that Mr. Fogg's hand gripped a knife tightly.
Phileas Fogg and his companions mingled at the back of the crowd as the funeral procession made its way to a stream.
On the bank of the stream, the body of the rajah who had been Aouda's husband lay on a large pile of carefully stacked wood.
From the back of the crowd, Mr. Fogg saw Aouda.
She was lying senseless beside her dead husband at the top of the funeral pyre. The Brahmin leader brought a torch.
The wood was heavily soaked in oil and instantly caught on fire.
Phileas Fogg let out a desperate moan, and Sir Francis and the guide seized him before he could rush onto the climbing flames.
He pushed them aside and stepped to the front of the crowd.
Just then a cry of terror arose. The old rajah was not dead!
He stood, took his wife in his arms, and, amidst a cloud of smoke, descended from the pyre.
Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis stood in shock.
The guide bowed his head, and all the Brahmins kneeled with their faces to the ground.
To Mr. Fogg's amazement, the rajah who had returned from the dead walked directly up to him.
"Let us be off!" he said. But it wasn't the rajah at all—it was Passepartout!
Ha! Were you surprised? If my plan had failed, I wouldn't be here talking to you now!
Cremation of the dead is very common in Hinduism.
A large funeral pyre is built, usually alongside a river, and the body of the deceased is placed on top.
With the help of a priest, the eldest son of the deceased will then light the fire.
After the cremation the deceased's soul is said to be naked.
Family members must perform various rites and ceremonies to provide the deceased with a "new spiritual body."
Eventually the bones of the deceased are collected and then either buried or placed into a river.
In the lingering darkness of the dawn, Passepartout had climbed up the funeral pyre from the back, where he couldn't be seen.
Then, profiting from the billows of smoke, he had braved the flames and saved the woman from death!
Without losing a moment, the four men disappeared into the jungle with Aouda.
They returned to the elephant and, thanks to their skillful guide, escaped quickly.
For the first hour, Passepartout laughed happily at his success.
Sir Francis shook his hand heartily. Fogg said simply, "Well done!" which, from him, was high praise, indeed.
Wrapped in a traveling blanket, Aouda rested on Kiouni's back until they reached the train station at Allahabad.
It was ten o'clock, and the journey to Calcutta would take 24 hours.
They would have just enough time to catch the steamer for Hong Kong on October 25 at noon.
Passepartout was sent to purchase some necessities for Aouda, including a dress and a shawl.
While he was away, Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis helped Aouda to a waiting room in the station.
They watched her anxiously, waiting for her to revive from her long slumber.
She had delicate cheeks, long silken lashes, fine white teeth, and smiling lips.
The men could not help but notice how charming she was.
Passepartout returned a little before the train was about to leave.
Outside the station Mr. Fogg was paying the guide, who stood with Kiouni.
"You have been a great help," he was saying.
"I have paid you for your service but not for your devotion.
Would you like to have this elephant? He is yours."
The guide's eyes glistened. "You are giving me a fortune!" he cried.
Mr. Fogg and his friends then boarded the train.
Kiouni trumpeted good-bye, and the guide waved as the train left the station.
Phileas Fogg, Sir Francis Cromarty, Passepartout, and Aouda were soon seated in their car, traveling at full speed.
It took two hours to reach the train's first stop at Benares, and during the journey, Aouda fully recovered from her drowsiness.
She was astonished to find herself in a car on a train, dressed in European clothing, and surrounded by strangers.
Her companions immediately told her what had transpired.
With tears in her eyes, she thanked her saviors repeatedly.
She knew, however, that her husband's family would not stop searching for her.
Danger would follow her as long as she remained in India.
When she explained that she had a merchant relative in Hong Kong, Mr. Fogg offered to escort her there safely.
At half-past 12, the train arrived in Benares. This was Sir Francis' destination.
He wished them all success on their journey and said good-bye.
From Benares the train passed through the valley of the Ganges River.
The travelers could see mountains; fields of barley, wheat, and corn; and jungles with green alligators.
They passed villages at the edges of thick forests and elephants bathing in sacred rivers.
Night fell and the train continued at full speed.
In the dark the passengers heard the roars of tigers, bears, and wolves, which fled at the sound of the locomotive.
The train reached Calcutta at seven in the morning on October 25.
According to Mr. Fogg's journal, that was the exact date scheduled for his arrival.
He was neither behind nor ahead of time.
The two days he had gained between London and Bombay had been lost in the journey across India.
But Phileas Fogg did not regret the loss in the least!
The train entered the station, and Passepartout jumped out first.
Mr. Fogg followed and held out his arm to help his fair companion down from the train.
Mr. Fogg intended to proceed at once to the Hong Kong steamer so that Aouda could get comfortably settled for the voyage.
He was unwilling to leave her side while she remained on dangerous ground.
Just as they were leaving the station, a policeman approached Mr. Fogg and said, "Mr. Phileas Fogg?"
"I am he," replied Fogg.
"Is this your servant?" asked the policeman, pointing to Passepartout.
"Yes," said Mr. Fogg.
"Both of you, be good enough to follow me," commanded the policeman.
Mr. Fogg betrayed no surprise or alarm.

The boat, carried forward by the wind, seemed to be flying over the waves.
Fix, seated below, kept apart from his fellow travelers.
He did not like to talk to the man whose favors he had been forced to accept.
"Once in the United States, what should I do?" he asked himself.
"Should I abandon my man? No! A hundred times, no! I will not lose sight of him for an hour!"
Mr. Fogg and Aouda ate with good appetites that evening.
Fix was invited to share their meal, which he accepted reluctantly.
To travel at this man's expense and live upon his provisions was distasteful to him.
Still, he was obliged to eat so he ate.
When the meal was over, he took Mr. Fogg aside and said, "Sir, you have been very kind to pay my way on this boat.
But . . . I must ask to pay my share."
"Let us not speak of that, sir," replied Mr. Fogg.
Fix was determined. "But, I insist—"
"No, sir," repeated Mr. Fogg. "I consider it part of my general expenses."
Fix bowed, returned to his cot, and did not speak again that evening.
At daybreak the next morning, the wind began to blow harder.
The sun had set in a red mist the night before.
John Bunsby had studied ocean weather long enough to know what it meant.
"We are going to have a rough wind," the captain said to Mr. Fogg.
"Is the wind north or south?" asked Mr. Fogg.
"South. Look! A typhoon is coming up!" said the captain.
"I am glad it's a typhoon from the south, as it will carry us forward!" said Mr. Fogg.
The captain took precautions and tied up all the sails.
The top masts were put away, and all hands went forward.
A single triangular sail of strong canvas was hoisted at the bow to keep the boat from turning into the wind. Then they waited.
John Bunsby had requested that all passengers go below, but Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Fix chose to remain on deck.
None of them wanted to feel imprisoned in a narrow space with very little air while the boat bounced about.
The storm and rain started around eight o'clock.
The [i@Tankadere@i] was lifted like a feather by a violent wind.
The boat flew northward, carried by monstrous waves.
The [i@Tankadere@i] was almost submerged numerous times by mountains of water that rose behind it, but the skill of the captain saved the boat.
The passengers were often bathed in a cold spray that was whipped by the wind. Fix cursed it.
Aouda kept her eyes fastened on her protector, whose coolness amazed her.
As for Mr. Fogg, he acted as if the typhoon was just part of his plan.
The [i@Tankadere@i] kept steady on its northward track.
The night was a terror, and it was a miracle that the boat did not sink.
Twice the boat would have gone down if the crew had not been constantly on the watch.
Aouda was exhausted, and more than once, Mr. Fogg rushed to protect her from the violence of the waves.
Day reappeared and the tempest raged just as fiercely.
By noon there were signs that the wind was calming, and the night was comparatively quiet.
Some of the sails were raised, and the [i@Tankadere@i] moved forward with speed again.
The next morning at dawn, the passengers could see the coast of Shanghai.
The wind and waves had grown much calmer.
At seven, they were still three miles from Shanghai when a long black smokestack,
crowned with a plume of white smoke, appeared on the waters near the coast.
"Blast our luck!" cried John Bunsby. "The Yokohama steamer has left the port!"
I heard that was quite a rough storm Mr. Fogg experienced!
I'm glad I missed that leg of the journey. I would have gotten terribly seasick.
Imagine going through all that and then missing the Yokohama steamer.

In response, the Japanese made Yokohama a port where foreign ships could dock.
Raw silk, tea, and many other products were traded through Yokohama, and this little town was transformed into a city.
Many Western influences first reached Japan through Yokohama, including the country's first daily newspaper and first railway.
The [i@Carnatic@i] departed at 6:30 p.m. on November 7 and steamed toward Yokohama, Japan.
The ship was completely booked, and only two staterooms in the rear were unoccupied, those reserved for Mr. Fogg and Aouda.
Shortly after Fix had left Passepartout in the opium den, two waiters lifted him to the bed reserved for smokers.
Three hours later he woke up and fought off the hypnotic influence of the drug.
He hurried to the steamer and, when he reached his room onboard, immediately passed out.
When Passepartout woke up the next morning, he staggered onto the deck, wondering what Mr. Fogg would say.
"At least I didn't miss the steamer, which is the most important thing!" he said to himself, as he sipped some strong black coffee.
Passepartout suddenly thought of Fix and how the man had left him in the tavern.
"As for that rascal, I hope we are rid of him," he said.
"A detective on the track of Mr. Fogg, accusing my master of robbing the Bank of England—ridiculous! Mr. Fogg is not a robber."
Passepartout finished his breakfast and then descended to the staterooms.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda were nowhere to be found! There was no luggage . . . nothing.
Passepartout wondered if he was even on the right ship.
He rushed to the purser and asked, "Am I on the [i@Carnatic@i]?"
"Yes, on the way to Yokohama," replied the purser, a little surprised.
"May I look at the passenger list?" asked Passepartout.
"Of course." The purser had the list with him and showed Passepartout.
When he had read every name, Passepartout fell thunderstruck on a seat.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda were not on the passenger list! Now he realized what had happened.
The time of departure had changed, and he had been unable to tell Mr. Fogg.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda had missed the steamer!
Passepartout felt sick to his stomach with rage.
He tore at his hair and vowed that, if he ever saw Fix again, he would even the score with him indeed!
After his anger calmed, Passepartout thought through his situation.
It was certainly not an attractive one.
He was on the way to Japan with no money.
And what was he going to do when he got there?
At dawn on November 13, the [i@Carnatic@i] reached the port of Yokohama.
Passepartout went ashore. He had nothing better to do than wander aimlessly through the city.
In the crowded streets, he saw all sorts of people: priests in white robes, police officers with black pointed hats,
sailors in blue cotton, and royal guards in stiff armor with long thin swords on their backs.
He also saw beautiful groves, tall sacred gates, bridges hidden in the midst of bamboo, and temples shaded by immense cedar trees.
By the next morning, hunger gnawed at Passepartout's empty stomach.
With no money, he thought of selling his precious family watch but changed his mind. He would rather starve first!
He decided he could earn some money as a vagabond performer but then thought he was too well dressed to be believable.
After a long search, he found a small shop that bought old clothes.
He asked the owner if he could exchange his European clothes for an old Japanese coat and a faded turban he saw in the window.
The owner also gave him a few pieces of silver in the trade.
Passepartout immediately found a food stand and ate what little breakfast he could afford.
"Now," he thought to himself, "I mustn't lose my head. I must consider how I am going to feed myself."
He walked toward the docks, having decided that passengers from visiting steamers would be the most generous customers.
On the way he was surprised to see a sign in English.
It read:
[i@Japanese Acrobats The Long Noses!@i]
[i@Come and see them before their departure to the United States! Grand Attraction!@i]
Passepartout was excited. He had been an acrobat in his youth.
If he was hired, he could find himself on the way to the United States, exactly where Mr. Fogg was headed!
A quarter of an hour later, Passepartout stopped before a large, colorful tent.
He entered and asked for the owner of the show.
Mr. Batulcar appeared immediately and interviewed Passepartout.
"You are pretty strong, eh?" asked Mr. Batulcar.
"Especially after a good meal!" responded Passepartout.
"And can you sing?" Mr. Batulcar asked.
"Yes," said Passepartout.
"But can you sing standing on your head, with a top spinning on your left foot and a sword balanced on your right?" asked Mr. Batulcar.

"You are hired!" exclaimed Mr. Batulcar.
Well, what a day! Wandering the streets of Yokohama with no money and then finding myself hired as an acrobat.
Yokohama certainly is a unique place, where East meets West!

Leaders have decided to model Japan's government, legal system, military, and economy on the West.
And according to a new policy, "knowledge shall be sought throughout the world."
So Japan has employed over three-thousand foreign experts in fields such as science, engineering,

Passepartout practiced with the Long Noses. The performers wore costumes from the Middle Ages,

The noses were made of bamboo and some were ten feet long!
Passepartout was a little embarrassed to be in a circus act again.
It reminded him too much of his youth.
But he cheered up, remembering his long nose was helping him to earn money for food.
He went onstage and took his place with the rest of the performers.
They balanced chairs, balls, and plates on the ends of their long noses.
Some climbed up to stand on their fellow performers' noses, performing handstands and acrobatic flips.
The theater was full, and the audience was delighted by the spectacle.
The grand finale was a feat called the "Great Pyramid."
A group of acrobats lay on the floor with their noses pointed at the ceiling.
A second group lay on the tips of the noses, and a third group climbed up on the noses of the second group.
A fourth group did the same, and a towering human pyramid was formed.
There was loud applause, and the orchestra began its fanfare when the pyramid began to tip from side to side.
One of the lower noses had vanished!
The pyramid tilted, tumbled, and collapsed like a house of cards. The missing performer was Passepartout.
"Master!" he cried as he jumped into the crowd and fell at the feet of one of the spectators.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda, who were seated in the audience, were shocked— as if they had been struck by lightning.
Passepartout was kneeling before them in his performer's costume.
"Passepartout! We are so happy to find you!" cried Aouda.
Mr. Batulcar was furious. He demanded compensation for his ruined show, and Mr. Fogg happily appeased him with a handful of banknotes.
The three traveling companions left the theater, together once again.
As they made their way through the streets of Yokohama, Aouda explained to Passepartout how they had finally found him.
"We reached Yokohama on the morning of November 14," she said.
"And Mr. Fogg immediately went on board the [i@Carnatic@i], which was still docked in the harbor.

"Yes. Luckily, I did not miss the steamer," said Passepartout.
"So we knew that you had arrived only the day before," Aouda continued.
"We visited the French and English consuls, but they had received no word of you.
After wandering through the streets, we began to despair.
Chance led us to Mr. Batulcar's theater.
We did not recognize you in your costume, but fortunately, you saw us!"
"You cannot imagine, madam, how happy I am to be back with you!" said Passepartout, smiling widely.
He turned to Mr. Fogg with a serious face.
"Sir, please forgive my poor behavior," he said.
"It was because of me that you missed the [i@Carnatic@i]. I beg your forgiveness.
I was drunk and did not tell you of the schedule change.
It will never happen again. Please believe me!"
"You are forgiven," said Mr. Fogg. "We will talk no more about it!"
They walked on in silence. Passepartout was relieved to be back with his master.
Aouda was very happy to see her friend once again.
Mr. Fogg was his usual self, as calm and distant as ever.
Passepartout then realized that, although Mr. Fogg and Aouda had missed the [i@Carnatic@i], somehow they had arrived in Yokohama only one day after him!
He turned to Aouda for an explanation.
She described their search for a boat in the port at Hong Kong and the perilous voyage they had survived.
Aouda then explained what had happened at Shanghai.
The Yokohama steamer was already underway as they approached the harbor.
At Mr. Fogg's request, the [i@Tankadere@i] signaled the steamer with its whistle.

Phileas Fogg quickly paid Captain Bunsby their agreed price, rewarding him with an additional 550 pounds.
The steamer let down a ladder, and Mr. Fogg and Aouda climbed aboard, followed by Mr. Fix.
Mr. Fogg listened politely as Aouda spoke, without adding a word of his own.
She finished her story as they reached the steamer, which was now docked in Yokohama harbor and bound for San Francisco.
Mr. Fogg then gave Passepartout the necessary funds to buy clothes that better suited his position.
Within an hour Passepartout had cut off his long nose, parted with his wings, and looked like his master's servant once more.
That was a neat little trick that Mr. Fogg arranged, wasn't it?
Putting the ship's flag at half-mast, I mean. In the days before radio, how did ships communicate?
Did they yell really loudly? Ha-ha! No, they used flags.
Flags are very important at sea. They can mean the difference between life and death!
Flags are flown when a ship is entering, or leaving, a harbor, and when a ship is sailing in foreign waters.
But why did the ship, the [i@Tankadere@i], fly its flag only halfway up the mast?

It means the ship is in trouble.
On land a flag at half-mast means that someone important has died.
There are special days when a country's flag is flown at half-mast too.
Why did this tradition develop?
Well, people decided that if a flag is halfway down, there is room for another "invisible" flag at the top of the flagpole.
This "invisible" flag represents and honors the person who has died.

According to the wager, his trip was to conclude by December 21.

Mr. Fogg's silent but generous nature impressed her.
The more time she spent with him, the more she began to feel emotions stronger than simple gratitude.
Her new feelings, however, did not seem to have any effect on Mr. Fogg.
Passepartout did not fail to notice the state of the lady's heart.
She was now as impatient as Fogg was over any delay in their journey.
He assured her that the most difficult part of the journey had already passed.
A railway train from San Francisco to New York and a steamer from New York to Liverpool would bring them to the end of their incredible travels.
Now that Fix was out of their way, no obstacles could slow their progress. At least, that's what Passepartout thought.
Detective Fix, however, was also on the [i@General Grant.@i]

"For now . . . yes," said Passepartout with satisfaction.
"Then let me have a word with you," said Fix.
"You have given me a thrashing, and I expected it.

"Aha!" cried Passepartout. "You are convinced he is an honest man!"

On December 2, the [i@General Grant@i] reached San Francisco.
Mr. Fogg had neither gained nor lost a single day.

At the first news vendor he saw, Mr. Fogg inquired when the next train left for New York.

"Perhaps I should purchase some rifles and revolvers while I am shopping, master?" asked Passepartout.

"I think it is a useless precaution, but do as you think best," replied Mr. Fogg.

Well, let me explain. When the explorer Christopher Columbus first arrived in America, he thought he was in India.
So when he encountered the Native Americans, he called them "Indians."
Like Europeans and Asians, the group of people known as Native American consists of hundreds of different cultures.
Two Native American tribes can differ as much as Asian people do.
Native Americans have lived in North America long before Europeans invaded the continent.
Since the arrival of Europeans, there has been a lot of fighting over land.
So far we haven't seen any of these wars, but our journey isn't over yet!
After being assaulted, Fix finally stood up.
He had an enormous bruise on his cheek, and his clothes were in tatters.
Luckily, Aouda had escaped unharmed. Mr. Fogg was covered in dust, but he was fine.
As soon as they were out of the crowd, Mr. Fogg thanked the detective.
"No thanks are necessary," replied Fix. "But let us go!"

Passepartout was there, waiting for his master and armed with half a dozen six-barreled revolvers.
When Passepartout saw Fix, he frowned. His expression changed, however, when Aouda explained their encounter with Colonel Proctor.

The backs of the seats were lowered, bedrolls were unpacked, and soon each traveler had a comfortable bed with clean sheets and a soft pillow.

That was quite a train ride—being delayed by thousands of buffalo, speeding over a collapsing bridge . . . Whew!
Aside from these incidents, our train journey has been quite enjoyable.
We have been traveling over America's prairies, large areas of open land like fields or meadows.
Tall grass and colorful wildflowers grow on the prairies, but there are very few trees.
In rainy areas the grass grows very tall, so tall that you could ride a horse and no one would see you! Now that's tall!
Many kinds of animals live here, including antelope, buffalo, and rabbits.
Buffalo are the largest mammals in North America, standing close to six feet high.
Even though they're big, they can run really fast, about 25 miles an hour.
So don't tease a buffalo because it'll catch you. And buffalo have horns. Ouch!

Mr. Fogg had no time to stop the courageous Passepartout, who crawled through a door and slipped under the train!
While bullets whizzed between the Indians and the passengers, smashing windows and puncturing seats,

He crawled forward from one car to the next until he reached the first car.
Hanging by one hand, he released the chains that attached the engine to the rest of the train.
The train shuddered violently, and the engine detached from the rest of the cars.
The engine raced ahead, but the cars began to slow.

At a quarter before nine, Phileas Fogg had walked into the great saloon and won his wager!
But where had he miscalculated? The cause of the error was simple.
Phileas Fogg had been traveling constantly eastward.
In journeying eastward he had gone toward the sun.
Therefore, each day was shortened by four minutes for every degree of longitude he crossed.
The circumference of the earth is measured in 360 degrees.
Three hundred and sixty degrees multiplied by four is exactly 24 hours.
Without realizing it Fogg had gained a day.
That evening Mr. Fogg, as tranquil as ever, said to Aouda, "Is our marriage still agreeable to you?"
"It is for me to ask that question," she said.
"You were ruined, but now you are rich again."
"Pardon me, madam," said Fogg. "But my fortune belongs to you.
If you had not suggested our marriage, Passepartout would not have gone to the reverend's house—"
"Dear Mr. Fogg!" she stopped him.
"Dear Aouda!" he replied with his whole heart.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda were married 48 hours later.
Passepartout, glowing with pride, gave the bride away.

Hooray! Mr. Fogg won his wager! Thank goodness for those funny lines on maps—longitude and latitude.
On a map, time zones are marked by lines of longitude.
The lines divide the globe into sections, or time zones.
Each section is one hour ahead of the section to its west and one hour behind the one to its east.
Look closely at the map. Can you see the lines that run across the globe east to west?
They are called lines of latitude. Do you know the most famous line of latitude?
I'll give you a clue. It's very hot there. That's right–the equator!
The equator runs right around the middle of the earth.
